   437	## Plugins
   438	
   439	Plugins extend the CLI with new verbs: any executable named `entire-<name>` on `$PATH` runs as `entire <name>`, kubectl-style — stdio passes through, exit codes propagate, no SDK or protocol required.
   440	
   441	```sh
   442	entire plugin search                                    # search the plugin index
   443	entire plugin browse                                    # browse the index interactively and install
   444	entire plugin install run                               # install by name (index lookup)
   445	entire plugin install https://github.com/you/entire-x   # install from any git host
   446	entire plugin install ./dist/entire-x                   # link a local build
   447	entire plugin list                                      # list what's installed
   448	entire run                                              # run an installed plugin
   449	entire plugin upgrade --all                             # update remote-installed plugins
   450	entire plugin doctor                                    # check for broken installs and missing dependencies
   451	entire plugin remove run
   452	```
   453	
   454	Remote installs are forge-agnostic: the newest stable semver tag is resolved over the git protocol (prereleases need an explicit `--pin`), and the platform's release asset is downloaded over HTTPS and verified against the release's `checksums.txt`. A release that publishes no checksums is refused unless you pass `--allow-unverified` — installing means making those bytes executable. `entire plugin doctor` re-checks installed binaries against the digests recorded at install time. Plugins can declare dependencies on other plugins in an `entire-plugin.yml`; missing ones are installed after a single confirmation.
   455	
   456	Discovery uses a git-synced catalog, [entireio/plugin-index](https://github.com/entireio/plugin-index) by default. Organizations can point the CLI at an internal catalog with the `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` environment variable or `--index`. It is deliberately not settable from a repository's committed settings: an index-listed plugin installs without a prompt, so a checked-out repo must not be able to choose the catalog.
   457	
   458	For the full contract — resolution rules, environment filtering, release-asset conventions, and how to author a plugin — see [External Commands](docs/architecture/external-commands.md).

   461	
   462	Entire uses two configuration files in the `.entire/` directory:
   463	
   464	### settings.json (Project Settings)
   465	
   466	Shared across the team, typically committed to git. This is what `entire enable` writes for a new repo:
   467	
   468	```json

   470	  "enabled": true,
   471	  "checkpoints": {
   472	    "primary": { "type": "git-refs" }
   473	  }
   474	}
   475	```
   476	
   477	### settings.local.json (Local Settings)
   478	
   479	Personal overrides, gitignored by default:
   480	
   481	```json
   482	{
   483	  "enabled": false,
   484	  "log_level": "debug"
   485	}
   486	```
   487

   489	
   490	| Option                                    | Values                                       | Description                                                                       |
   491	| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   492	| `enabled`                                 | `true`, `false`                              | Enable/disable Entire                                                             |
   493	| `log_level`                               | `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`             | Logging verbosity                                                                 |
   494	| `checkpoints.primary.type`                | `git-refs`                                   | Checkpoint storage backend — written by `entire enable`, see [Checkpoint Storage](#checkpoint-storage) |
   495	| `telemetry`                               | `true`, `false`                              | Send anonymous usage statistics to Posthog                                        |

   500	| `strategy_options.checkpoint_remote`      | `{"provider": "github", "repo": "org/repo"}` | Push checkpoint data to a separate repo (see below)                               |

   510	
   511	Each agent stores its hook configuration in its own directory. When you run `entire enable`, hooks are installed in the appropriate location for each selected agent:

   514	| ---------------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------- |

   526	### Checkpoint Remote
   527	
   528	By default, checkpoint data rides along with your own pushes — but only to **one** remote, the elected checkpoint sync remote. Entire picks it in this order:
   529	
   530	1. `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote`, if set. This is fail-closed: if it names a remote that isn't configured, checkpoints don't sync.
   531	2. A remote captured from your own habits: the first push whose target matches the branch's declared push destination elects that remote, announces it on stderr, and carries the checkpoints. The first capture sticks.
   532	3. `origin`
   533	4. The sole remote, if the repo has exactly one
   534	5. The first remote in `.git/config` order
   535	
   536	A push to any *other* remote carries no checkpoint data. `entire status` shows the current destination, where it came from, and how many checkpoints are unpushed. This matters if you push code to several remotes: checkpoints go to exactly one of them.
   537	
   538	If instead you want checkpoint data in a separate repo (e.g., a private repo for a public project), configure `checkpoint_remote` with a structured provider and repo. A dedicated `checkpoint_remote` is addressed directly and is exempt from the single-remote election above:

   540	```json
   541	{
   542	  "strategy_options": {
   543	    "checkpoint_remote": {
   544	      "provider": "github",
   545	      "repo": "myorg/checkpoints-private"
   546	    }
   547	  }
   548	}
   549	```
   550	
   551	Or via the CLI:
   552	
   553	```bash
   554	entire enable --checkpoint-remote github:myorg/checkpoints-private
   555	```
   556	
   557	Entire derives the git URL automatically using the same protocol (SSH or HTTPS) as your push remote. It will:
   558	
   559	- Fetch existing checkpoint data locally if the remote has it and you don't (one-time)
   560	- Push checkpoint data to the checkpoint repo instead of your default push remote
   561	- Ignore the setting if it looks inherited rather than yours, and fall back to `origin` (or, failing that, the remote you are pushing to). `checkpoint_remote` is normally committed in `.entire/settings.json`, so cloning or forking a project inherits it — without this, a contributor's session data would be pushed into the upstream project's checkpoint repo. A setting is treated as yours when it lives in the gitignored `.entire/settings.local.json`, or when your `origin` **and every push URL** of the remote you are pushing to are owned by the same account or org as the checkpoint repo. Requiring the push destination too covers contributors who cloned the upstream repo and added their own fork, where `origin` belongs to the upstream project rather than to them; requiring every push URL covers mirror-style remotes that fan out to several repositories
   562	- If your checkpoint repo is owned by a different account or org than `origin`, configure it in `.entire/settings.local.json` so it is always honored
   563	- If the remote is unreachable, warn and continue without blocking your main push

   623	- Entire supports Pi coding agent (Preview). Pi uses a TypeScript extension instead of a JSON hook config. Subagent capture is not currently available.
   624	
   625	## Security & Privacy
   626	
   627	**Your session transcripts are stored in your git repository**, in the [per-checkpoint refs](#checkpoint-storage) described above. If your repository is public, this data is visible to anyone.
   628	
   629	Entire automatically redacts detected secrets (API keys, tokens, credentials) from transcripts and metadata before writing a checkpoint, but redaction is best-effort.
   630	
   631	The temporary shadow branches used during a session get the same redaction for transcripts and metadata, but their **code-file snapshots are raw blobs of your working tree**, so a secret hardcoded in your source appears unredacted there. Entire never pushes shadow branches — don't push them manually. See [docs/security-and-privacy.md](docs/security-and-privacy.md) for the full picture, including the configurable scanner layers, opt-in PII redaction, and the OpenAI Privacy Filter pass.
   632	
   633	## Troubleshooting
   634	
   635	### Common Issues
   636	
   637	| Issue                              | Solution                                                          |
   638	| ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
   639	| "Not a git repository"             | Navigate to a Git repository first                                |
   640	| "Entire is disabled"               | Run `entire enable`                                               |

   279	the work across multiple PRs. When you are ready to start, the repo ships a
   280	skill that walks through the full pipeline:

   284	| Full pipeline | [`.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/SKILL.md`](.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/SKILL.md) | Run all three phases sequentially |
   285	| Research | [`.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/research.md`](.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/research.md) | Analyze the target agent and map to the protocol |
   286	| Write tests | [`.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/write-tests.md`](.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/write-tests.md) | Scaffold the binary, wire protocol + lifecycle coverage |
   287	| Implement | [`.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/implement.md`](.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/implement.md) | Build the binary using protocol compliance first, lifecycle second, unit tests last |

   296	| OpenCode | `.opencode/plugins/` | "Build an external agent" |

   301	exists, but the `mise` tasks are the contract for anything non-standard.

   304	
   305	## Submitting a Pull Request
   306	
   307	### Before You Submit
   308	
   309	- **Related issue exists and is approved**: Your PR references an issue
   310	  where a maintainer has acknowledged the approach. (Exceptions: typo
   311	  corrections, wording-only updates, and maintainer-scoped starter tasks.)

   313	- **Linting passes**: `golangci-lint` clean.
   314	- **Tests pass**: `mise run test` for unit tests; `mise run test:e2e` if
   315	  your change is lifecycle-relevant.
   316	- **Tests included**: New Go code and protocol behavior should ship with
   317	  accompanying tests at the right layer.
   318	- **Entire checkpoint trailers included**: See
   319	  [Using Entire While Contributing](#using-entire-while-contributing).

   324

   326	2. **Open a PR** against the `main` branch.

   328	   are affected, summarize what changed and what testing you did.
   329	4. **Address Copilot feedback**: See [Responding to Automated Review](#responding-to-automated-review).
   330	5. **Wait for maintainer review.**

   334	## Responding to Automated Review
   335	
   336	A Copilot reviewer comments on every PR with feedback on code quality,
   337	potential bugs, and project conventions.
   338	
   339	**Read and respond to every Copilot comment.** PRs with unaddressed Copilot
   340	feedback will not move to maintainer review.
   341

   343	- **Disagree**: Reply explaining your reasoning. Copilot isn't always right.
   344	- **Question**: Ask for clarification.

   350	## Using Entire While Contributing
   351	
   352	We use Entire on Entire. When contributing to this repo, install the Entire
   353	CLI and let it capture your coding sessions. This gives us valuable
   354	dogfooding data and helps improve the tool.

   359	[installation docs](https://docs.entire.io/cli/installation)) and verify with
   360	`entire version`. Entire is already configured in this repository, so there is
   361	no need to run `entire enable`.

   364	
   365	All commits should include `Entire-Checkpoint` trailers from your sessions.
   366	These are added automatically by the `prepare-commit-msg` hook when Entire is
   367	enabled. The trailers link your commits to session metadata on the
   368	`entire/checkpoints/v1` branch.
   369	
   370	### Sessions Branch
   371	
   372	When you push your PR branch, Entire can automatically push the
   373	`entire/checkpoints/v1` branch alongside it (if `push_sessions` is enabled in
   374	your settings). Including it lets maintainers see the session context behind
   375	your changes.

    79	#### Migrating an old `cli` Scoop install (package rename)
    80	
    81	The Scoop package was renamed from `cli` to `entire`. If your install is still registered as the old `cli` package, run the migration below. It installs the new package before removing the old one, so the old install is only removed once the new one is in place (`scoop reset` re-links the shared `entire.exe` and `git-remote-entire.exe` shims). Run it where `entire` is **not** running — a live `entire.exe` locks its own shim, so Scoop can't relink or uninstall it mid-run:
    82	
    83	```powershell
    84	cmd.exe /D /C "scoop install entire/entire && scoop uninstall entire/cli && scoop reset entire"
    85	```
    86	
    87	If the first step fails with "couldn't find manifest", your bucket clone predates the renamed package — run `scoop update` to refresh it, then retry the command above. Nothing is removed until the install succeeds, so a failed attempt leaves your existing install working.

   117	## Release Channels
   118	
   119	Entire currently ships two release channels:
   120	
   121	- `stable`: recommended for most users. Stable releases change less often and are the default for Homebrew, Scoop, and `install.sh`.
   122	- `nightly`: prerelease builds for users who want the latest changes earlier. Nightlies are published more frequently and may include newer, less-proven changes than stable.
   123	
   124	How to use each channel:
   125	
   126	- Homebrew (one-time setup): `brew tap entireio/tap && brew trust entireio/tap`
   127	- Homebrew stable: `brew install --cask entire`
   128	- Homebrew nightly: `brew install --cask entire@nightly`
   129	- `install.sh` stable: `curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash`
   130	- `install.sh` nightly: `curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly`
   131	- Scoop: currently supports `stable` only via `scoop install entire/entire`

   133	## Typical Workflow
   134	
   135	### 1. Enable Entire in Your Repository
   136	
   137	```
   138	entire enable
   139	```
   140	
   141	On a repo that has not been enabled yet, `entire enable` runs the initial enable flow: it creates Entire settings, installs git hooks, and prompts you to choose which agent hooks to install. To enable a specific agent non-interactively, use `entire enable --agent <name>` (for example, `entire enable --agent cursor`).
   142	
   143	After setup:
   144	
   145	- Use `entire enable` to turn Entire back on if the repo is currently disabled.
   146	- Use `entire agent` to add or remove agents.
   147	- Use `entire configure` to update non-agent settings (telemetry, hooks, checkpoint remote, summary provider).
   148	
   149	The hooks capture session data as you work. Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit. Your code commits stay clean, Entire never creates commits on your active branch. Session metadata is stored outside your branch's history, in the checkpoint storage described under [Checkpoint Storage](#checkpoint-storage).
   150	
   151	### 2. Work with Your AI Agent
   152	
   153	Just use one of your AI agents as before. Entire runs in the background, tracking your session:
   154	
   155	```
   156	entire status  # Check current session status anytime
   157	```
   158	
   159	### 3. Resume a Previous Session
   160	
   161	To restore the latest checkpointed session metadata for a branch:
   162	
   163	```
   164	entire session resume <branch>
   165	```
   166	
   167	Entire checks out the branch, restores the latest checkpointed session metadata (one or more sessions), and prints command(s) to continue.
   168	
   169	### 4. Disable Entire (Optional)
   170	
   171	```
   172	entire disable
   173	```
   174	
   175	Removes the git hooks. Your code and commit history remain untouched.

   177	## Key Concepts
   178	
   179	### Sessions
   180	
   181	A **session** represents a complete interaction with your AI agent, from start to finish. Each session captures all prompts, responses, files modified, and timestamps.
   182	
   183	The session ID is the unique identifier the agent itself provides — Entire never mints its own — so an ID you see in `entire session list` is the same one the agent uses. The format is the agent's to choose: most supply a UUID (e.g. `019efea2-b46a-7cbc-be01-4c13460f5019`), while OpenCode uses `ses_`-prefixed IDs.
   184	
   185	Sessions are stored separately from your code commits, in the repo's checkpoint storage.
   186	
   187	### Checkpoints
   188	
   189	A **checkpoint** is a snapshot within a session—a "save point" in your work.
   190	
   191	Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit, and the commit carries an `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` trailer linking the two.
   192	
   193	**Checkpoint IDs** are 26-character ULIDs (e.g. `REDACTED`), which sort by creation time. Checkpoints written by older versions of Entire carry a legacy 12-character hex ID (e.g. `a3b2c4d5e6f7`); both formats stay readable in the same repo, and you can pass either to any command that takes a checkpoint ID.
   194	
   195	### Checkpoint Storage
   196	
   197	Checkpoints live in your repository's own git object store, never in your branch's history. Each checkpoint is its own git ref:
   198	
   199	```
   200	refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>
   201	```
   202	
   203	The ref points at a commit whose tree *is* that checkpoint — `metadata.json`, the per-session transcript files, and any subagent task records. `<shard>` is the last two characters of the ID, which keeps the refs evenly distributed.
   204	
   205	Because checkpoints are independent refs, they are written, pushed, and fetched independently. There is no shared branch tip for concurrent sessions to contend on, and a reader can fetch exactly the one checkpoint it needs instead of a whole history. A checkpoint written on another machine is fetched on demand the first time you read it.
   206	
   207	`entire enable` sets this up; there is nothing to configure. It is recorded in `.entire/settings.json` as:
   208	
   209	```json
   210	{
   211	  "checkpoints": {
   212	    "primary": { "type": "git-refs" }
   213	  }
   214	}
   215	```
   216	
   217	Inspect what a repo has locally with plain git, or through Entire:
   218	
   219	```bash
   220	git for-each-ref refs/entire/checkpoints    # the raw refs
   221	entire checkpoint list                      # checkpoints on this branch
   222	entire checkpoint explain <id>              # one checkpoint in full
   223	```

   437	## Plugins
   438	
   439	Plugins extend the CLI with new verbs: any executable named `entire-<name>` on `$PATH` runs as `entire <name>`, kubectl-style — stdio passes through, exit codes propagate, no SDK or protocol required.
   440	
   441	```sh
   442	entire plugin search                                    # search the plugin index
   443	entire plugin browse                                    # browse the index interactively and install
   444	entire plugin install run                               # install by name (index lookup)
   445	entire plugin install https://github.com/you/entire-x   # install from any git host
   446	entire plugin install ./dist/entire-x                   # link a local build
   447	entire plugin list                                      # list what's installed
   448	entire run                                              # run an installed plugin
   449	entire plugin upgrade --all                             # update remote-installed plugins
   450	entire plugin doctor                                    # check for broken installs and missing dependencies
   451	entire plugin remove run
   452	```
   453	
   454	Remote installs are forge-agnostic: the newest stable semver tag is resolved over the git protocol (prereleases need an explicit `--pin`), and the platform's release asset is downloaded over HTTPS and verified against the release's `checksums.txt`. A release that publishes no checksums is refused unless you pass `--allow-unverified` — installing means making those bytes executable. `entire plugin doctor` re-checks installed binaries against the digests recorded at install time. Plugins can declare dependencies on other plugins in an `entire-plugin.yml`; missing ones are installed after a single confirmation.
   455	
   456	Discovery uses a git-synced catalog, [entireio/plugin-index](https://github.com/entireio/plugin-index) by default. Organizations can point the CLI at an internal catalog with the `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` environment variable or `--index`. It is deliberately not settable from a repository's committed settings: an index-listed plugin installs without a prompt, so a checked-out repo must not be able to choose the catalog.
   457	
   458	For the full contract — resolution rules, environment filtering, release-asset conventions, and how to author a plugin — see [External Commands](docs/architecture/external-commands.md).

   462	Entire uses two configuration files in the `.entire/` directory:

   467	
   468	```json

   470	  "enabled": true,
   471	  "checkpoints": {
   472	    "primary": { "type": "git-refs" }
   473	  }
   474	}
   475	```
   476	
   477	### settings.local.json (Local Settings)
   478	
   479	Personal overrides, gitignored by default:
   480	
   481	```json
   482	{
   483	  "enabled": false,
   484	  "log_level": "debug"
   485	}
   486	```

   489	
   490	| Option                                    | Values                                       | Description                                                                       |
   491	| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   492	| `enabled`                                 | `true`, `false`                              | Enable/disable Entire                                                             |
   493	| `log_level`                               | `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`             | Logging verbosity                                                                 |
   494	| `checkpoints.primary.type`                | `git-refs`                                   | Checkpoint storage backend — written by `entire enable`, see [Checkpoint Storage](#checkpoint-storage) |
   495	| `telemetry`                               | `true`, `false`                              | Send anonymous usage statistics to Posthog                                        |

   509	### Agent Hook Configuration
   510	
   511	Each agent stores its hook configuration in its own directory. When you run `entire enable`, hooks are installed in the appropriate location for each selected agent:
   512	
   513	| Agent            | Hook Location                 | Format            |
   514	| ---------------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------- |
   515	| Claude Code      | `.claude/settings.json`       | JSON hooks config |
   516	| Codex            | `.codex/hooks.json`           | JSON hooks config |
   517	| Copilot CLI      | `.github/hooks/entire.json`   | JSON hooks config |
   518	| Cursor           | `.cursor/hooks.json`          | JSON hooks config |
   519	| Factory AI Droid | `.factory/settings.json`      | JSON hooks config |
   520	| Gemini CLI       | `.gemini/settings.json`       | JSON hooks config |
   521	| OpenCode         | `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts` | TypeScript plugin |
   522	| Pi               | `.pi/extensions/entire/index.ts` | TypeScript extension |
   523	
   524	You can enable multiple agents at the same time — each agent's hooks are independent. Entire detects which agents are active by checking for installed hooks, not by a setting in `settings.json`.
   525	
   526	### Checkpoint Remote
   527	
   528	By default, checkpoint data rides along with your own pushes — but only to **one** remote, the elected checkpoint sync remote. Entire picks it in this order:
   529	
   530	1. `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote`, if set. This is fail-closed: if it names a remote that isn't configured, checkpoints don't sync.
   531	2. A remote captured from your own habits: the first push whose target matches the branch's declared push destination elects that remote, announces it on stderr, and carries the checkpoints. The first capture sticks.
   532	3. `origin`
   533	4. The sole remote, if the repo has exactly one
   534	5. The first remote in `.git/config` order
   535	
   536	A push to any *other* remote carries no checkpoint data. `entire status` shows the current destination, where it came from, and how many checkpoints are unpushed. This matters if you push code to several remotes: checkpoints go to exactly one of them.
   537	
   538	If instead you want checkpoint data in a separate repo (e.g., a private repo for a public project), configure `checkpoint_remote` with a structured provider and repo. A dedicated `checkpoint_remote` is addressed directly and is exempt from the single-remote election above:
   539	
   540	```json
   541	{
   542	  "strategy_options": {
   543	    "checkpoint_remote": {
   544	      "provider": "github",
   545	      "repo": "myorg/checkpoints-private"
   546	    }
   547	  }
   548	}
   549	```
   550	
   551	Or via the CLI:
   552	
   553	```bash
   554	entire enable --checkpoint-remote github:myorg/checkpoints-private
   555	```
   556	
   557	Entire derives the git URL automatically using the same protocol (SSH or HTTPS) as your push remote. It will:
   558	
   559	- Fetch existing checkpoint data locally if the remote has it and you don't (one-time)
   560	- Push checkpoint data to the checkpoint repo instead of your default push remote
   561	- Ignore the setting if it looks inherited rather than yours, and fall back to `origin` (or, failing that, the remote you are pushing to). `checkpoint_remote` is normally committed in `.entire/settings.json`, so cloning or forking a project inherits it — without this, a contributor's session data would be pushed into the upstream project's checkpoint repo. A setting is treated as yours when it lives in the gitignored `.entire/settings.local.json`, or when your `origin` **and every push URL** of the remote you are pushing to are owned by the same account or org as the checkpoint repo. Requiring the push destination too covers contributors who cloned the upstream repo and added their own fork, where `origin` belongs to the upstream project rather than to them; requiring every push URL covers mirror-style remotes that fan out to several repositories
   562	- If your checkpoint repo is owned by a different account or org than `origin`, configure it in `.entire/settings.local.json` so it is always honored
   563	- If the remote is unreachable, warn and continue without blocking your main push
   564	
   565	#### `ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN`
   566	
   567	`ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN` allows you to provide a dedicated token for checkpoint repository operations, without modifying the credentials used for your primary repository.
   568	
   569	When this environment variable is set, Entire behaves as follows:
   570	
   571	- Injects the token into HTTPS Git operations used for checkpoint fetch and push
   572	- If `checkpoint_remote` is configured:
   573	  - Prefers an HTTPS URL for the checkpoint remote when a token is present, even if the repository’s `origin` uses SSH
   574	- If `checkpoint_remote` is not configured:
   575	  - Falls back to using the default `origin` remote
   576	- If `checkpoint_remote` configuration cannot be loaded:
   577	  - Falls back to `origin`
   578	  - If `origin` is a valid SSH or HTTPS Git remote, Entire converts it to an HTTPS URL to enable token-based authentication
   579	
   580	### Auto-Summarization
   581	
   582	When enabled, Entire automatically generates AI summaries for checkpoints at commit time. Summaries capture intent, outcome, learnings, friction points, and open items from the session.
   583	
   584	```json
   585	{
   586	  "strategy_options": {
   587	    "summarize": {
   588	      "enabled": true
   589	    }
   590	  }
   591	}
   592	```
   593	
   594	Summaries are also generated on demand, with or without this setting, by `entire checkpoint explain --generate`.
   595	
   596	**Which agent writes them.** By default Claude Code (`claude` on your `PATH`, model `sonnet`). Set a different one with `summary_generation.provider` — `claude-code`, `codex`, `copilot-cli`, `cursor`, `gemini`, or `pi`, plus an optional `summary_generation.model` hint:
   597	
   598	```bash
   599	entire configure --summarize-provider codex
   600	```
   601	
   602	`opencode` and `factoryai-droid` cannot generate summaries. Whichever provider you pick must be installed and authenticated.

   605	
   606	- The configured provider's CLI installed and authenticated
   607	- Summary generation is non-blocking: failures are logged but don't prevent commits

   610	
   611	Local settings override project settings field-by-field. `entire status --detailed` shows the state of each settings file.
   612	
   613	Two exceptions to field-by-field merging:
   614

   625	## Security & Privacy
   626	
   627	**Your session transcripts are stored in your git repository**, in the [per-checkpoint refs](#checkpoint-storage) described above. If your repository is public, this data is visible to anyone.

   629	Entire automatically redacts detected secrets (API keys, tokens, credentials) from transcripts and metadata before writing a checkpoint, but redaction is best-effort.

225	### How It Works
   226	
   227	```
   228	Your Branch                      Checkpoint storage
   229	     │                                  │
   230	     ▼                                  │
   231	[Base Commit]                           │
   232	     │                                  │
   233	     │  ┌─── Agent works ───┐           │
   234	     │  │  Turn 1           │           │
   235	     │  │  Turn 2           │           │
   236	     │  │  Turn 3           │           │
   237	     │  └───────────────────┘           │
   238	     │                                  │
   239	     ▼                                  ▼
   240	[Your Commit] ─────────────────► [Checkpoint]
   241	  Entire-Checkpoint: <id>          (transcript, prompts,
   242	     │                              files touched, tokens)
   243	     ▼
   244	```
   245	
   246	Work in progress is held on a short-lived shadow branch as you go. When you commit, that work is condensed into a permanent checkpoint and linked to your commit by an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.
   247	
   248	### Strategy
   249	
   250	Entire uses a manual-commit strategy that keeps your git history clean:
   251	
   252	- **No commits on your branch** — Entire never creates commits on the active branch
   253	- **Safe on any branch** — works on main, master, and feature branches alike
   254	- **Metadata stored separately** — session data lives in per-checkpoint refs, never in your branch's history
   255	
   256	### Git Worktrees
   257	
   258	Entire works seamlessly with [git worktrees](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree). Each worktree has independent session tracking, so you can run multiple AI sessions in different worktrees without conflicts.
   259	
   260	### Concurrent Sessions
   261	
   262	Multiple AI sessions can run on the same commit. If you start a second session while another has uncommitted work, Entire warns you and tracks them separately. Both sessions' checkpoints are preserved, and a commit condenses every session with pending work in that worktree.
   263	
   264	## Headless & CI Authentication
   265	
   266	By default `entire login` opens a browser to sign in and stores tokens in the OS keyring (macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service, Windows Credential Manager). Machines without a usable browser or keyring — headless servers, containers, minimal VMs, CI runners — have two supported paths:
   267	
   268	### Interactive login on a headless machine
   269	
   270	Sign-in itself already handles this: with no interactive terminal, or over SSH, `entire login` switches to the device-code flow on its own and prints an approval URL you can open on any machine. `entire login --device` forces that flow explicitly. Only token *storage* needs an override — use the file-backed store:
   271	
   272	```bash
   273	ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file entire login
   274	```
   275	
   276	Tokens are written with `0600` permissions to `tokens.json` in your Entire config directory (`~/.config/entire` by default). Override the location with `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE_PATH`. Set `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file` persistently (e.g. in your shell profile) so later commands read from the same store.
   277	
   278	### Non-interactive automation (CI, workload identity)
   279	
   280	Skip login and storage entirely by injecting a token per invocation:
   281	
   282	```bash
   283	ENTIRE_TOKEN=<login-or-sa-session-JWT> entire ...
   284	```
   285	
   286	`ENTIRE_TOKEN` bypasses stored credentials; the CLI derives the control-plane endpoint from the token itself. Nothing is written to disk. This is the right path for CI pipelines and service accounts.
   287	
   288	> **Seeing `save login` / `failed to unlock correct collection` errors from `entire login`?** That's the OS keyring being unavailable — use one of the two paths above.
   289	
   290	## Commands Reference
   291	
   292	Descriptions below are the commands' own summaries. `entire help` always reflects the installed binary; `entire agent-help` is the machine-readable version agents read.
   293	
   294	### Setup
   295	
   296	| Command            | Description                                                                        |
   297	| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   298	| `entire enable`    | Enable Entire in current repository                                                |
   299	| `entire disable`   | Disable Entire in current repository                                               |

Only token *storage* needs an override — use the file-backed store:
   271	
   272	```bash
   273	ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file entire login
   274	```
   275	
   276	Tokens are written with `0600` permissions to `tokens.json` in your Entire config directory (`~/.config/entire` by default). Override the location with `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE_PATH`. Set `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file` persistently (e.g. in your shell profile) so later commands read from the same store.
   277	
   278	### Non-interactive automation (CI, workload identity)
   279	
   280	Skip login and storage entirely by injecting a token per invocation:
   281	
   282	```bash
   283	ENTIRE_TOKEN=<login-or-sa-session-JWT> entire ...
   284	```
   285	
   286	`ENTIRE_TOKEN` bypasses stored credentials; the CLI derives the control-plane endpoint from the token itself. Nothing is written to disk. This is the right path for CI pipelines and service accounts.
   287	
   288	> **Seeing `save login` / `failed to unlock correct collection` errors from `entire login`?** That's the OS keyring being unavailable — use one of the two paths above.
   289	
   290	## Commands Reference
   291	
   292	Descriptions below are the commands' own summaries. `entire help` always reflects the installed binary; `entire agent-help` is the machine-readable version agents read.
   293	
   294	### Setup
   295	
   296	| Command            | Description                                                                        |
   297	| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   298	| `entire enable`    | Enable Entire in current repository                                                |
   299	| `entire disable`   | Disable Entire in current repository                                               |

1	---
     2	name: entire-external-agent
     3	description: >
     4	  Run all three external agent binary phases sequentially: research, write-tests,
     5	  and implement using black-box-first TDD across protocol compliance, lifecycle
     6	  integration, and unit tests. Accepts an optional argument to run a single phase:
     7	  research, write-tests, or implement.
     8	---
     9	
    10	## Plan Mode Override
    11	
    12	If plan mode is active when this skill is invoked, call ExitPlanMode immediately
    13	before doing anything else. This skill has its own multi-phase procedure
    14	(Research → Write-Tests → Implement) that IS the plan. Do not wrap it in a
    15	separate planning workflow — execute the phases directly.
    16	
    17	# External Agent Binary — Full Pipeline
    18	
    19	Build a standalone external agent binary that implements the Entire CLI external agent protocol.
    20	
    21	The current test split is:
    22	
    23	1. **Protocol compliance** lives in `external-agents-tests`.
    24	2. **Lifecycle integration** lives in this repo's `e2e/` harness.
    25	3. **Unit tests** live in each agent module.
    26	
    27	Do not add new generic protocol tests under this repo's `e2e/` directory.
    28	
    29	## Parameters
    30	
    31	Collect these before starting if the user did not provide them:
    32	
    33	| Parameter | Description | Default |
    34	|-----------|-------------|---------|
    35	| `AGENT_NAME` | Human-readable name (for example, `Windsurf`) | User-provided |
    36	| `AGENT_SLUG` | Binary suffix for `entire-agent-<slug>` | Kebab-case of `AGENT_NAME` |
    37	| `LANGUAGE` | Implementation language | `Go` |
    38	| `PROJECT_DIR` | Agent directory to create or edit | `./agents/entire-agent-<slug>` |
    39	| `ENTIRE_BIN` | Path to the Entire CLI binary for lifecycle testing | `entire` from `PATH` or `E2E_ENTIRE_BIN` |
    40	
    41	## Phase Selection
    42	
    43	- `/entire-external-agent research` runs only Phase 1.
    44	- `/entire-external-agent write-tests` runs only Phase 2.
    45	- `/entire-external-agent implement` runs only Phase 3.
    46	- `/entire-external-agent` runs all three phases in order.
    47	
    48	If a single phase is requested, still collect the shared parameters first.
    49	
    50	## Protocol Spec
    51	
    52	Use the protocol specification at:
    53	`https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture/external-agent-protocol.md`
    54	
    55	If the user gives a different spec location explicitly, use that instead.
    56	
    57	## Core Rule: Black-Box-First TDD
    58	
    59	1. **Protocol compliance is the contract.** The binary must pass the shared `external-agents-tests` suite.
    60	2. **Lifecycle tests prove real integration.** The repo-local `e2e/` harness covers the Entire + real-agent workflow and stays separate from generic protocol checks.
    61	3. **Unit tests are written last.** After protocol and lifecycle behavior are working, add unit tests to lock down parsing, hooks, and file handling.
    62	4. **Watch failures before fixing them.** Run the failing test first so you know what behavior the code must satisfy.
    63	5. **Keep the fix scoped.** Implement only the behavior needed for the current failure, then rerun.
    64	
    65	## Pipeline
    66	
    67	### Phase 1: Research
    68	
    69	Discover the target agent's hook mechanism, transcript format, session layout, CLI entrypoints, and lifecycle prerequisites. Produce `<PROJECT_DIR>/AGENT.md` with the protocol mapping and any real-CLI requirements needed for lifecycle tests.
    70	
    71	Use `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/research.md`.
    72	
    73	Expected output:
    74	- `<PROJECT_DIR>/AGENT.md`
    75	
    76	### Phase 2: Write Tests
    77	
    78	Scaffold the binary and the test surfaces you will need:
    79	
    80	- agent module structure under `<PROJECT_DIR>`
    81	- protocol compliance expectations compatible with `external-agents-tests`
    82	- lifecycle adapter wiring in this repo's `e2e/` harness
    83	- optional compliance fixtures if the agent benefits from stronger black-box detect or transcript assertions
    84	
    85	Use `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/write-tests.md`.
    86	
    87	Expected output:
    88	- compiling binary scaffold
    89	- any needed lifecycle adapter files under `e2e/agents/`
    90	- optional fixture file paths documented in `<PROJECT_DIR>/AGENT.md` or `README.md`
    91	
    92	### Phase 3: Implement
    93	
    94	Implement until:
    95	
    96	- the binary passes protocol compliance
    97	- lifecycle tests pass when the required CLIs are available
    98	- unit tests cover the important internal behaviors
    99	
   100	Use `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/implement.md`.
   101	
   102	Expected output:
   103	- fully working binary
   104	- passing unit tests
   105	- passing protocol compliance
   106	- passing lifecycle integration where dependencies are available
   107	
   108	## Final Summary
   109	
   110	At the end, summarize:
   111	
   112	- agent name and binary name
   113	- implementation language
   114	- declared capabilities
   115	- protocol compliance status
   116	- lifecycle test status
   117	- unit test coverage
   118	- installation instructions
   119	- any remaining gaps

     5	  for building an external agent binary. Use /entire-external-agent research
     6	  or /entire-external-agent:research when you only need the research phase.
     7	---
     8	
     9	# Research Procedure
    10	
    11	Assess a target agent's capabilities and produce a protocol mapping for building an external agent binary.
    12	
    13	## Prerequisites
    14	
    15	Ensure the following parameters are available (from the orchestrator or user):
    16	- `AGENT_NAME` — Human-readable agent name
    17	- `AGENT_SLUG` — Kebab-case slug for the binary name
    18	- `PROJECT_DIR` — Where the project will be created
    19	
    20	## Phase 1: Understand the External Agent Protocol
    21	
    22	Read the protocol specification to understand what subcommands and response formats the binary must implement.
    23	
    24	**Protocol spec:**
    25	1. Read `https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture/external-agent-protocol.md` — full protocol spec (subcommands, JSON schemas, capabilities)
    26	2. Read `https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/main/cmd/entire/cli/agent/external/types.go` — JSON response type definitions
    27	3. Read `https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/main/cmd/entire/cli/agent/external/external.go` — how the CLI invokes each subcommand (args, stdin, expected stdout)
    28	
    29	If the user provides a different protocol spec location explicitly, read that instead.
    30	
    31	Key things to note:
    32	- Which subcommands are always required vs. capability-gated
    33	- The JSON schema for each response type
    34	- The HookInput, AgentSession, and Event object formats
    35	- Environment variables set on every invocation (`ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT`, `ENTIRE_PROTOCOL_VERSION`)
    36	
    37	## Phase 2: Investigate the Target Agent
    38	
    39	Ask the user: "Do you have documentation or specs for the target agent's hook/lifecycle system? Or should I auto-research?"
    40	
    41	### If user provides docs:
    42	Read the provided docs and extract:
    43	- Hook/lifecycle mechanism (how to register callbacks)
    44	- Session management (where sessions are stored, how IDs work)
    45	- Transcript format and location
    46	- Configuration file format and location
    47	
    48	### If auto-research:
    49	
    50	#### Step 1: Binary probing
    51	
    52	Run non-destructive CLI checks. Record PASS/WARN/FAIL for each:
    53	
    54	| Check | Command | PASS | FAIL |
    55	|-------|---------|------|------|
    56	| Binary present | `command -v <agent-binary>` | Found | Not found |
    57	| Help output | `<agent-binary> --help` or `<agent-binary> help` | Available | No help |
    58	| Version info | `<agent-binary> --version` | Available | N/A |
    59	| Hook keywords | Scan help for: hook, lifecycle, callback, event, trigger, pre-, post-, plugin, extension | Found | None found |
    60	| Session keywords | Scan help for: session, resume, continue, history, transcript, context | Found | None found |
    61	| Config directory | Check `~/.<agent-slug>/`, `~/.config/<agent-slug>/`, `./<agent-slug>/`, `./.${agent-slug}/` | Found | None found |
    62	
    63	#### Step 2: Documentation search
    64	
    65	Use web search to find:
    66	- The agent's official hook/plugin/extension documentation
    67	- How to register lifecycle callbacks
    68	- Session/transcript storage format and location
    69	- Configuration file format
    70	
    71	#### Step 3: Config and session directory exploration
    72	
    73	If a config directory was found:
    74	1. List its contents (non-destructively)
    75	2. Look for settings files (JSON, YAML, TOML)
    76	3. Look for session/history directories
    77	4. Look for transcript files and determine their format
    78	
    79	#### Step 4: Map agent concepts to protocol subcommands
    80	
    81	For each protocol subcommand, determine:
    82	- Whether the agent has a native concept that maps to it
    83	- How to implement it (which native API/config/file to use)
    84	- Whether it's straightforward or requires workarounds
    85	
    86	Create a mapping table:
    87	
    88	| Subcommand | Native Concept | Implementation Notes | Feasibility |
    89	|-----------|---------------|---------------------|-------------|
    90	| `info` | — | Static metadata, always implementable | Required |
    91	| `detect` | — | Check for binary or config | Required |
    92	| `get-session-id` | (agent's session ID mechanism) | ... | Required |
    93	| `get-session-dir` | (agent's session directory) | ... | Required |
    94	| `resolve-session-file` | (how agent stores sessions) | ... | Required |
    95	| `read-session` | (session data format) | ... | Required |
    96	| `write-session` | (session data persistence) | ... | Required |
    97	| `read-transcript` | (transcript file location) | ... | Required |
    98	| `chunk-transcript` | (raw bytes, language-generic) | Base64 chunking | Required |
    99	| `reassemble-transcript` | (reverse of chunk) | Base64 reassembly | Required |
   100	| `format-resume-command` | (agent's resume mechanism) | ... | Required |
   101	| `parse-hook` | (agent's native hook events) | ... | If hooks capable |
   102	| `install-hooks` | (agent's hook config format) | ... | If hooks capable |
   103	| `uninstall-hooks` | (reverse of install) | ... | If hooks capable |
   104	| `are-hooks-installed` | (check hook config) | ... | If hooks capable |
   105	| `get-transcript-position` | (file size/position) | ... | If transcript analyzer |
   106	| `extract-modified-files` | (parse transcript for file ops) | ... | If transcript analyzer |
   107	| `extract-prompts` | (parse transcript for user msgs) | ... | If transcript analyzer |
   108	| `extract-summary` | (parse transcript for summaries) | ... | If transcript analyzer |
   109	
   110	#### Step 5: Select capabilities
   111	
   112	Based on the mapping, determine which capabilities the binary should declare:
   113	- `hooks` — Can the agent be configured to call external commands on lifecycle events?
   114	- `transcript_analyzer` — Does the agent produce parseable transcripts?
   115	- `transcript_preparer` — Does the transcript need pre-processing?
   116	- `token_calculator` — Does the transcript contain token usage data?
   117	- `text_generator` — Can the agent's LLM be invoked for text generation?
   118	- `hook_response_writer` — Does the agent support writing messages back via hooks?
   119	- `subagent_aware_extractor` — Does the agent spawn subagents with their own transcripts?
   120	
   121	## Phase 3: Verification Script
   122	
   123	Docs tend to be out of date. Before writing the one-pager, create a verification script that captures real payloads from the target agent to confirm Phase 2 findings.
   124	
   125	Based on Phase 2 findings, create an **agent-specific** test script:
   126	
   127	```
   128	<PROJECT_DIR>/scripts/verify-<AGENT_SLUG>.sh
   129	```
   130	
   131	The script is tailored to the specific agent's hook mechanism (not a generic template). Adapt the hook wiring section based on what Phase 2 discovered.
   132	
   133	**Script structure:**
   134	
   135	```bash
   136	#!/usr/bin/env bash
   137	set -euo pipefail
   138	
   139	AGENT_NAME="..."
   140	AGENT_SLUG="..."
   141	AGENT_BIN="..."
   142	PROBE_DIR="<PROJECT_DIR>/.probe-${AGENT_SLUG}-$(date +%s)"
   143	```
   144	
   145	**Required sections:**
   146	
   147	1. **Static checks** — Re-runnable binary/version/help checks from Phase 2
   148	2. **Hook wiring** — Create workspace-local config that intercepts the agent's hooks and dumps stdin JSON to `$PROBE_DIR/captures/<event-name>-<timestamp>.json`. Use the agent's native hook config format discovered in Phase 2.
   149	3. **Run modes:**
   150	   - `--run-cmd '<cmd>'` — Automated: launch agent with a non-interactive prompt, wait, collect captures
   151	   - `--manual-live` — Interactive: user runs agent manually, presses Enter when done
   152	4. **Capture collection** — List and pretty-print all captured payload files
   153	5. **Cleanup** — Restore original config (unless `--keep-config`)
   154	6. **Verdict** — PASS/WARN/FAIL per lifecycle event + summary
   155	
   156	**Important:** The hook wiring must be non-destructive — back up any existing config before modifying, and restore it on cleanup.
   157	
   158	### Phase 3a: Execute & Analyze
   159	
   160	Run the script and analyze the captured payloads:
   161	
   162	1. **Execute**: `chmod +x <PROJECT_DIR>/scripts/verify-<AGENT_SLUG>.sh && <PROJECT_DIR>/scripts/verify-<AGENT_SLUG>.sh --manual-live`
   163	2. **For each captured payload**: show the file path, decoded JSON, and which protocol subcommand it informs
   164	3. **Update Phase 2 findings**: If captured payloads differ from documentation (field names, nesting, missing fields), update the mapping table with ground-truth values from the captures
   165	4. **Lifecycle mapping**: native hook name → protocol event type, validated against real captures
   166	
   167	If the script cannot be run (agent not installed, auth required, sandbox restrictions), follow the Blocker Handling procedure and note in the one-pager that findings are doc-based only and not verified.
   168	
   169	### Phase 3b: Verify Stored Data Completeness
   170	
   171	Hook payloads tell you *when* events fire, but not whether the agent's stored data (sessions, transcripts) actually contains usable content. IDEs often store placeholder text in session files while keeping the real data in a separate location (execution logs, databases, caches). **You must verify this before writing the one-pager.**
   172	
   173	#### Step 1: Use distinctive prompts in a test repo
   174	
   175	Create a test repo and run 2-3 prompts with greppable content:
   176	- Ask the agent to summarize a URL (produces a known response)
   177	- Ask it to create a file (produces tool calls + file writes)
   178	- Ask a follow-up question (produces a multi-turn session)
   179	
   180	These give you specific strings to search for across all storage locations.
   181	
   182	#### Step 2: Inspect session/transcript files for actual content
   183	
   184	Read the session files identified in Phase 2 and check each assistant message:
   185	- Does it contain the **actual response text** you saw in the UI, or just a placeholder like `"On it."`, `"Working..."`, `"Sure"`, or empty string?
   186	- Are **tool calls** recorded with their names, inputs, and outputs?
   187	- Is the `completion` / `response` / `content` field populated or empty?
   188	- Do `promptLogs` or similar fields contain the full model output?
   189	
   190	**If assistant content is placeholder-only, the agent stores real data elsewhere.** Proceed to Step 3.
   191	
   192	#### Step 3: Find ALL recently modified files
   193	
   194	Before running a prompt, create a timestamp marker. After the prompt completes, find everything the IDE touched:
   195	
   196	```bash
   197	touch /tmp/before-marker
   198	# ... run your prompt in the IDE ...
   199	find ~/Library/Application\ Support/<agent>/ -type f -newer /tmp/before-marker 2>/dev/null
   200	# Linux: find ~/.config/<agent>/ -type f -newer /tmp/before-marker
   201	```
   202	
   203	This reveals hidden storage that documentation may not mention — execution logs, per-turn action traces, content-addressed caches, etc.
   204	
   205	#### Step 4: Search for your distinctive response
   206	
   207	Grep the entire IDE data directory for the known response text from your test prompts:
   208	
   209	```bash
   210	grep -rl "your distinctive response text" ~/Library/Application\ Support/<agent>/ 2>/dev/null
   211	```
   212	
   213	This definitively locates where the real data lives. Read the matching files to understand their format.
   214	
   215	#### Step 5: Map the IDE's internal ID system
   216	
   217	Look for cross-referencing IDs that link session files to the real data:
   218	- Session IDs, execution IDs, conversation IDs, workspace IDs
   219	- How they cross-reference (e.g., session file has `executionId` → execution log has matching field)
   220	- Whether IDs are deterministic (computable from workspace path or session ID) or opaque (require scanning)

   225	### How It Works
   226	
   227	```
   228	Your Branch                      Checkpoint storage
   229	     │                                  │
   230	     ▼                                  │
   231	[Base Commit]                           │
   232	     │                                  │
   233	     │  ┌─── Agent works ───┐           │
   234	     │  │  Turn 1           │           │
   235	     │  │  Turn 2           │           │
   236	     │  │  Turn 3           │           │
   237	     │  └───────────────────┘           │
   238	     │                                  │
   239	     ▼                                  ▼
   240	[Your Commit] ─────────────────► [Checkpoint]
   241	  Entire-Checkpoint: <id>          (transcript, prompts,
   242	     │                              files touched, tokens)
   243	     ▼
   244	```
   245	
   246	Work in progress is held on a short-lived shadow branch as you go. When you commit, that work is condensed into a permanent checkpoint and linked to your commit by an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.
   247	
   248	### Strategy
   249	
   250	Entire uses a manual-commit strategy that keeps your git history clean:
   251	
   252	- **No commits on your branch** — Entire never creates commits on the active branch
   253	- **Safe on any branch** — works on main, master, and feature branches alike
   254	- **Metadata stored separately** — session data lives in per-checkpoint refs, never in your branch's history
   255	
   256	### Git Worktrees
   257	
   258	Entire works seamlessly with [git worktrees](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree). Each worktree has independent session tracking, so you can run multiple AI sessions in different worktrees without conflicts.
   259	
   260	### Concurrent Sessions
   261	
   262	Multiple AI sessions can run on the same commit. If you start a second session while another has uncommitted work, Entire warns you and tracks them separately. Both sessions' checkpoints are preserved, and a commit condenses every session with pending work in that worktree.
   263	
   264	## Headless & CI Authentication
   265	
   266	By default `entire login` opens a browser to sign in and stores tokens in the OS keyring (macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service, Windows Credential Manager). Machines without a usable browser or keyring — headless servers, containers, minimal VMs, CI runners — have two supported paths:
   267	
   268	### Interactive login on a headless machine
   269	
   270	Sign-in itself already handles this: with no interactive terminal, or over SSH, `entire login` switches to the device-code flow on its own and prints an approval URL you can open on any machine. `entire login --device` forces that flow explicitly. Only token *storage* needs an override — use the file-backed store:
   271	
   272	```bash
   273	ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file entire login
   274	```
   275	
   276	Tokens are written with `0600` permissions to `tokens.json` in your Entire config directory (`~/.config/entire` by default). Override the location with `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE_PATH`. Set `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file` persistently (e.g. in your shell profile) so later commands read from the same store.
   277	
   278	### Non-interactive automation (CI, workload identity)
   279	
   280	Skip login and storage entirely by injecting a token per invocation:
   281	
   282	```bash
   283	ENTIRE_TOKEN=<login-or-sa-session-JWT> entire ...
   284	```
   285	
   286	`ENTIRE_TOKEN` bypasses stored credentials; the CLI derives the control-plane endpoint from the token itself. Nothing is written to disk. This is the right path for CI pipelines and service accounts.
   287	
   288	> **Seeing `save login` / `failed to unlock correct collection` errors from `entire login`?** That's the OS keyring being unavailable — use one of the two paths above.
   289

    97	| `read-transcript` | (transcript file location) | ... | Required |
    98	| `chunk-transcript` | (raw bytes, language-generic) | Base64 chunking | Required |
    99	| `reassemble-transcript` | (reverse of chunk) | Base64 reassembly | Required |
   100	| `format-resume-command` | (agent's resume mechanism) | ... | Required |
   101	| `parse-hook` | (agent's native hook events) | ... | If hooks capable |
   102	| `install-hooks` | (agent's hook config format) | ... | If hooks capable |
   103	| `uninstall-hooks` | (reverse of install) | ... | If hooks capable |
   104	| `are-hooks-installed` | (check hook config) | ... | If hooks capable |
   105	| `get-transcript-position` | (file size/position) | ... | If transcript analyzer |
   106	| `extract-modified-files` | (parse transcript for file ops) | ... | If transcript analyzer |
   107	| `extract-prompts` | (parse transcript for user msgs) | ... | If transcript analyzer |
   108	| `extract-summary` | (parse transcript for summaries) | ... | If transcript analyzer |
   109	
   110	#### Step 5: Select capabilities
   111	
   112	Based on the mapping, determine which capabilities the binary should declare:
   113	- `hooks` — Can the agent be configured to call external commands on lifecycle events?
   114	- `transcript_analyzer` — Does the agent produce parseable transcripts?
   115	- `transcript_preparer` — Does the transcript need pre-processing?
   116	- `token_calculator` — Does the transcript contain token usage data?
   117	- `text_generator` — Can the agent's LLM be invoked for text generation?
   118	- `hook_response_writer` — Does the agent support writing messages back via hooks?
   119	- `subagent_aware_extractor` — Does the agent spawn subagents with their own transcripts?
   120	
   121	## Phase 3: Verification Script
   122	
   123	Docs tend to be out of date. Before writing the one-pager, create a verification script that captures real payloads from the target agent to confirm Phase 2 findings.
   124	
   125	Based on Phase 2 findings, create an **agent-specific** test script:
   126	
   127	```
   128	<PROJECT_DIR>/scripts/verify-<AGENT_SLUG>.sh
   129	```
   130	
   131	The script is tailored to the specific agent's hook mechanism (not a generic template). Adapt the hook wiring section based on what Phase 2 discovered.
   132	
   133	**Script structure:**
   134	
   135	```bash
   136	#!/usr/bin/env bash
   137	set -euo pipefail
   138	
   139	AGENT_NAME="..."
   140	AGENT_SLUG="..."
   141	AGENT_BIN="..."
   142	PROBE_DIR="<PROJECT_DIR>/.probe-${AGENT_SLUG}-$(date +%s)"
   143	```
   144	
   145	**Required sections:**
   146	
   147	1. **Static checks** — Re-runnable binary/version/help checks from Phase 2
   148	2. **Hook wiring** — Create workspace-local config that intercepts the agent's hooks and dumps stdin JSON to `$PROBE_DIR/captures/<event-name>-<timestamp>.json`. Use the agent's native hook config format discovered in Phase 2.
   149	3. **Run modes:**
   150	   - `--run-cmd '<cmd>'` — Automated: launch agent with a non-interactive prompt, wait, collect captures
   151	   - `--manual-live` — Interactive: user runs agent manually, presses Enter when done
   152	4. **Capture collection** — List and pretty-print all captured payload files
   153	5. **Cleanup** — Restore original config (unless `--keep-config`)
   154	6. **Verdict** — PASS/WARN/FAIL per lifecycle event + summary
   155	
   156	**Important:** The hook wiring must be non-destructive — back up any existing config before modifying, and restore it on cleanup.
   157	
   158	### Phase 3a: Execute & Analyze
   159	
   160	Run the script and analyze the captured payloads:
   161	
   162	1. **Execute**: `chmod +x <PROJECT_DIR>/scripts/verify-<AGENT_SLUG>.sh && <PROJECT_DIR>/scripts/verify-<AGENT_SLUG>.sh --manual-live`
   163	2. **For each captured payload**: show the file path, decoded JSON, and which protocol subcommand it informs
   164	3. **Update Phase 2 findings**: If captured payloads differ from documentation (field names, nesting, missing fields), update the mapping table with ground-truth values from the captures
   165	4. **Lifecycle mapping**: native hook name → protocol event type, validated against real captures
   166	
   167	If the script cannot be run (agent not installed, auth required, sandbox restrictions), follow the Blocker Handling procedure and note in the one-pager that findings are doc-based only and not verified.
   168	
   169	### Phase 3b: Verify Stored Data Completeness
   170	
   171	Hook payloads tell you *when* events fire, but not whether the agent's stored data (sessions, transcripts) actually contains usable content. IDEs often store placeholder text in session files while keeping the real data in a separate location (execution logs, databases, caches). **You must verify this before writing the one-pager.**
   172	
   173	#### Step 1: Use distinctive prompts in a test repo
   174	
   175	Create a test repo and run 2-3 prompts with greppable content:
   176	- Ask the agent to summarize a URL (produces a known response)
   177	- Ask it to create a file (produces tool calls + file writes)
   178	- Ask a follow-up question (produces a multi-turn session)
   179	
   180	These give you specific strings to search for across all storage locations.
   181	
   182	#### Step 2: Inspect session/transcript files for actual content
   183	
   184	Read the session files identified in Phase 2 and check each assistant message:
   185	- Does it contain the **actual response text** you saw in the UI, or just a placeholder like `"On it."`, `"Working..."`, `"Sure"`, or empty string?
   186	- Are **tool calls** recorded with their names, inputs, and outputs?
   187	- Is the `completion` / `response` / `content` field populated or empty?
   188	- Do `promptLogs` or similar fields contain the full model output?
   189	
   190	**If assistant content is placeholder-only, the agent stores real data elsewhere.** Proceed to Step 3.
   191	
   192	#### Step 3: Find ALL recently modified files
   193	
   194	Before running a prompt, create a timestamp marker. After the prompt completes, find everything the IDE touched:
   195	
   196	```bash
   197	touch /tmp/before-marker
   198	# ... run your prompt in the IDE ...
   199	find ~/Library/Application\ Support/<agent>/ -type f -newer /tmp/before-marker 2>/dev/null
   200	# Linux: find ~/.config/<agent>/ -type f -newer /tmp/before-marker
   201	```
   202	
   203	This reveals hidden storage that documentation may not mention — execution logs, per-turn action traces, content-addressed caches, etc.
   204	
   205	#### Step 4: Search for your distinctive response
   206	
   207	Grep the entire IDE data directory for the known response text from your test prompts:
   208	
   209	```bash
   210	grep -rl "your distinctive response text" ~/Library/Application\ Support/<agent>/ 2>/dev/null
   211	```
   212	
   213	This definitively locates where the real data lives. Read the matching files to understand their format.
   214	
   215	#### Step 5: Map the IDE's internal ID system
   216	
   217	Look for cross-referencing IDs that link session files to the real data:
   218	- Session IDs, execution IDs, conversation IDs, workspace IDs
   219	- How they cross-reference (e.g., session file has `executionId` → execution log has matching field)
   220	- Whether IDs are deterministic (computable from workspace path or session ID) or opaque (require scanning)

    62	Your job in this repo is to make the agent easy to validate there:

    84	Read these files before editing:

   106	cd <PROJECT_DIR>

   109	go test ./...
   110	
   111	cd /path/to/repo/e2e

   113	```

   115	Also run one failing compliance pass against the built binary:
   116	
   117	```bash
   118	external-agents-tests verify ./entire-agent-<slug>
   119	```
   120	
   121	## Step 5: Commit Gate
   122	
   123	Create a commit once:

   134	- files created under `<PROJECT_DIR>`
   135	- lifecycle adapter files added or updated under `e2e/`
   136	- optional compliance fixture paths
   137	- commands run and their status

     2	description: Build standalone external agent binaries for the Entire CLI using E2E-first TDD
     3	alwaysApply: false
     4	---
     5	
     6	# External Agent Builder
     7	
     8	This repository includes a skill for building standalone external agent binaries that implement the Entire CLI's external agent protocol.
     9	
    10	## When to Activate
    11	
    12	Use this when the user asks to "build an external agent", "create an agent binary", "external agent plugin", or wants to research, scaffold, implement, or validate an Entire CLI external agent.
    13	
    14	## Skill Files
    15	
    16	Read these files for detailed procedures:
    17	
    18	- **Full pipeline:** `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/SKILL.md` — runs all three phases sequentially
    19	- **Research:** `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/research.md` — analyze the target agent
    20	- **Write tests:** `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/write-tests.md` — scaffold binary + E2E harness
    21	- **Implement:** `.claude/skills/entire-external-agent/implement.md` — E2E-first TDD, unit tests last
    22	
    23	## Protocol Spec
    24	
    25	The external agent protocol is defined at:
    26	`https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture/external-agent-protocol.md`
    27	
    28	## Tool Mapping
    29	
    30	The skill files reference Claude Code tool names. Map them to Cursor equivalents:
    31	
    32	| Skill references | Cursor equivalent |
    33	|-----------------|-----------------|
    34	| `TodoWrite` | Cursor's task/plan tracking |
    35	| `Task` / subagent launches | Cursor's agent mode |
    36	| `Skill` tool | Read the skill file directly |
    37	| `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Glob`, `Grep`, `Bash` | Native Cursor tools |
    38	import path from 'path';
    39	import { fileURLToPath } from 'url';

   134	          // Reset per-session tracking state when switching sessions.
   135	          if (currentSessionID !== session.id) {
   136	            seenUserMessages.clear()
   137	            messageStore.clear()
   138	            currentModel = null
   139	          }
   140	          currentSessionID = session.id
   141	          await callHook("session-start", {
   142	            session_id: session.id,
   143	          })
   144	          break
   145	        }
   146	
   147	        case "message.updated": {
   148	          const msg = (event as any).properties?.info
   149	          if (!msg) break
   150	          // Store message metadata (role, time, tokens, etc.)
   151	          messageStore.set(msg.id, msg)
   152	          // Track model from assistant messages
   153	          if (msg.role === "assistant" && msg.modelID) {
   154	            currentModel = msg.modelID
   155	          }
   156	          break
   157	        }
   158	
   159	        case "message.part.updated": {
   160	          const part = (event as any).properties?.part
   161	          if (!part?.messageID) break
   162	
   163	          // Fire turn-start on the first text part of a new user message
   164	          const msg = messageStore.get(part.messageID)
   165	          if (msg?.role === "user" && part.type === "text" && !seenUserMessages.has(msg.id)) {
   166	            seenUserMessages.add(msg.id)
   167	            const sessionID = msg.sessionID ?? currentSessionID
   168	            if (sessionID) {
   169	              await callHook("turn-start", {
   170	                session_id: sessionID,
   171	                prompt: part.text ?? "",
   172	                model: currentModel ?? "",
   173	              })
   174	            }
   175	          }
   176	          break
   177	        }
   178	
   179	        case "session.status": {
   180	          // session.status fires in both TUI and non-interactive (run) mode.
   181	          // session.idle is deprecated and not reliably emitted in run mode.
   182	          const props = (event as any).properties
   183	          if (props?.status?.type !== "idle") break
   184	          const sessionID = props?.sessionID ?? currentSessionID
   185	          if (!sessionID) break
   186	          // Use sync variant: `opencode run` exits on the same idle event,
   187	          // so an async hook would be killed before completing.
   188	          callHookSync("turn-end", {
   189	            session_id: sessionID,
   190	            model: currentModel ?? "",
   191	          })
   192	          break
   193	        }
   194	
   195	        case "session.compacted": {
   196	          const sessionID = (event as any).properties?.sessionID
   197	          if (!sessionID) break
   198	          await callHook("compaction", {
   199	            session_id: sessionID,
   200	          })
   201	          break
   202	        }
   203	
   204	        case "session.deleted": {
   205	          const session = (event as any).properties?.info
   206	          if (!session?.id) break
   207	          seenUserMessages.clear()
   208	          messageStore.clear()
   209	          currentSessionID = null
   210	          // Use sync variant: session-end may fire during shutdown.
   211	          callHookSync("session-end", {
   212	            session_id: session.id,
   213	          })
   214	          break
   215	        }
   216	
   217	        case "server.instance.disposed": {
   218	          // Fires when OpenCode shuts down (TUI close or `opencode run` exit).
   219	          // session.deleted only fires on explicit user deletion, not on quit,
   220	          // so this is the only reliable way to end sessions on exit.
   221	          if (!currentSessionID) break
   222	          const sessionID = currentSessionID
   223	          seenUserMessages.clear()
   224	          messageStore.clear()
   225	          currentSessionID = null
   226	          // Use sync variant: this is the last event before process exit.
   227	          callHookSync("session-end", {
   228	            session_id: sessionID,
   229	          })
   230	          break
   231	        }
   232	      }
   233	    },
   234	  }

    45	```
    46	
    47	Do not start by adding new protocol tests to this repo.

    55	3. implement the minimum fix
    56	4. rerun until it passes

    60	- `info` and capability declarations
    61	- `detect`
    62	- session helpers
    63	- transcript chunking and reassembly
    64	- session read/write behavior
    65	- hooks capability
    66	- transcript analysis capability
    67

    71	
    72	```bash

    81	- `tmux` for interactive scenarios

    92	- rewind and checkpoint interactions
    93	- interactive session handling
    94	
    95	Keep protocol fixes in the agent binary itself. Keep real-CLI orchestration fixes in the lifecycle adapter.
